research_notes: Released in Japan 15 October 1961 (Toshiba-EMI). First heard 16 August 1961 on NHK programme Yume de Aimashō. English-market title 'Sukiyaki' has no connection to the lyrics (it is a beef dish). US Billboard Hot 100 no. 1 in 1963. Year 1961 is the Japanese release year.

original_format: Vocal, often unaccompanied or with folk ensemble
secondary_associations: UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage | North Korea (shared tradition)
research_notes: Korean folk song with about 3,600 variants of some 60 versions, all sharing a refrain similar to 'arirang, arirang, arariyo'. Inscribed twice on the UNESCO ICH list (South Korea 2012, North Korea 2014). Origin commonly associated with Jeongseon, Gangwon; first mention cited by Keith Howard in a 1756 manuscript. National Archives of Korea notes multiple origin theories and no agreed-upon date. Country filed as South Korea (research source of the UNESCO 2012 file); the song is shared across the peninsula. Year left empty.

composer: Traditional (Edo-period urban melody; Meiji-period koto arrangement)
songwriter: Traditional; present lyrics attached in the Meiji period
research_notes: Edo-period urban melody, not an ancient court piece. Melody arranged by Ongaku Torishirabe-gakari included in Collection of Japanese Koto Music, 1888, for beginning koto students at the Tokyo Academy of Music. Present lyrics attached in the Meiji period; a new first verse published by the Ministry of Education in 1941. Year left empty (traditional melody; 1888 is a published koto arrangement, not the origin).
Jiangnan folk song, usually dated to the 18th-century Qianlong reign (Qing); some argue Ming (pre-1644). Chinese Wikipedia: originally called 鲜花调. Year left empty. Many regional variants.

composer: 湯尼 / 翁清溪 (Tony / Weng Ching-hsi)
research_notes: Originally recorded by Chen Fen-lan, album Dreamland, Li Ge Records, May 1973; also by Liu Guan-lin, November 1973. Made famous by Teresa Teng on Love Songs of the Island, Vol. 4: Love in Hong Kong (Polydor Hong Kong, 19 December 1977). Japanese Wikipedia confirms lyricist Sun Yi and composer Tony (Weng Qingxi). Year 1977 is Teng's reference recording; composition/first recording is 1973.

title_english: Kawa no nagare no yō ni (Like the Flow of the River)
research_notes: Single released 11 January 1989 by Nippon Columbia; recorded 28 October 1988. Lyrics Yasushi Akimoto, music Akira Mitake, arrangement Kōji Ryūzaki. Hibari Misora's last single released in her lifetime. Artist also romanised Hibari Misora.

original_instruments: Ryūteki | Hichiriki | Shō | Koto | Biwa | Kakko | Shōko | Taiko
research_notes: Best-known gagaku kangen piece, usually in hyōjō; banshiki-chō and ōshiki-chō versions also exist. Japanese Wikipedia cites a 966 court exit performance in Fusō ryakki. Origin is disputed (made in Japan, or transmitted from Tang/Khotan). Dance is obsolete. Later Western-orchestra and piano-and-orchestra works use the melody but are separate compositions. Also written 越殿楽.

title_original: プラスティック・ラヴ
original_instruments: Electric guitar | Electric piano | Bass | Drums
research_notes: Album track on Variety, released 25 April 1984 (Moon/Alfa Moon); produced and arranged by Tatsuro Yamashita. Single release 25 March 1985. Japanese Wikipedia names electric piano (Yasuharu Nakanishi), bass (Hiroki Ito) and drums (Jun Aoyama), with Yamashita on guitar. Year is the album release. Artist also romanised Mariya Takeuchi.

title_english: Tsugaru Kaikyō fuyugeshiki (Tsugaru Strait Winter Scene)
research_notes: Single released 1 January 1977 (Nippon Columbia). Lyrics Yu Aku, music and arrangement Takashi Miki. First issued on the November 1976 album 365日恋もよう. Japanese Wikipedia names tenor saxophonist Masaaki Sano on the introduction. Artist also romanised Sayuri Ishikawa. Year is the single release.

Instrumental by Yukihiro Takahashi on Solid State Survivor (Alfa, 25 September 1979); produced by Haruomi Hosono. Japanese single June 1980. A chiptune of the piece was later used as the theme of the 1982 arcade game Super Locomotive; the composition itself predates that game. Official Alfa music video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Yxep-gS-Btg. Year is the album release.

Track on Happy End album 風街ろまん (URC, 20 November 1971). Lyrics Takashi Matsumoto, music Haruomi Hosono, who also sings. Album credits list acoustic guitar, bass, organ and vocals (Hosono) and drums (Matsumoto); recorded 6 September 1971. Later used in the film Lost in Translation; the song was not written for that film. Year is the album release.

title_english: Haru no umi (The Sea in Spring)
research_notes: Koto and shakuhachi duet by Michio Miyagi, composed at the end of 1929 for the 1930 imperial poetry topic. Premiere that year with shakuhachi player Seifū Yoshida at Hibiya Public Hall. Victor recording with Miyagi and Yoshida released December 1930 (NDL). A violin arrangement of the shakuhachi part by Renée Chemet followed her 1932 visit. Year is the composition year stated by these sources. New Japanese music (新日本音楽), not Western art music.

Six-section instrumental danmono for koto in hirajōshi. Traditionally attributed to Yatsuhashi Kengyō (1614–1685). Kotobank and Japanese Wikipedia note that living Ikuta and Yamada versions may not be his own piece and that some Edo sources credit his student Kitajima Kengyō. No exact year is entered. Later played with shamisen, kokyū and shakuhachi.

Hokkaido herring-fishery work song, the okiage ondo of the Japan Sea coast (Shakotan to Yoichi). Unaccompanied in its work form. Around 1935 the min'yō singer Imai Kōzan fitted shamisen and selected verses for stage use. Kotobank traces the call to Aomori stevedore song brought north with the fishery. No composition year.

title_original: 真夜中のドア〜Stay With Me
research_notes: Debut single by Miki Matsubara, Canyon Records 7-inch W-17, released 5 November 1979. Lyrics Tokiko Miura, music and arrangement Tetsuji Hayashi. Also on the album Pocket Park. Year is the single release.

original_instruments: Piano | Strings | Bass | Drums | Guitar | Synthesizer
research_notes: Written by Hikaru Utada. Single released 28 April 1999 (Toshiba EMI); title track of the March 1999 album. Arrangement and strings by Kei Kawano. English Wikipedia describes piano, bass, drums, guitars and synthesizers in the arrangement; a published solo piano edition was not found. Used as the theme of the TBS drama Majo no jōken; the song was already an album track. Year is the single release.

Fourth single by Sheena Ringo, Toshiba EMI TOCT-22010, released 27 October 1999. Words and music by Ringo; arrangement Seiji Kameda. Oricon and Universal Music Japan confirm the date and catalogue number. Used as an ending theme on Nippon TV's FUN; it is her own single, not a commissioned score. Year is the single release.

Major-label debut single, Meldac, 1 May 1987. Words and music by vocalist Hiroto Kōmoto. The band's Wikipedia discography lists the same date. An Oricon product page gives 21 February 1988 for a later catalogue number (10MD-5); the 1987 date is the one used here. Year is the single release.

Lullaby of nursemaid girls from Itsuki, Kuma District, Kumamoto. Kotobank and Japanese Wikipedia agree it is a local moriko-uta. The melody widely known after 1945 was transcribed by Yūji Koseki and recorded by commercial singers (Teru Kiku, 1953) and differs from the village version. No composition year.

subgenre: New music (ニューミュージック)
original_instruments: Piano | Bass | Electric guitar | Drums | Keyboards
research_notes: Written by Yumi Arai (later Yumi Matsutoya). B-side of the single Kitto ieru (5 November 1973) and title track of the album released 20 November 1973 (Express). Official discography credits her piano and Caramel Mama: Haruomi Hosono (bass), Shigeru Suzuki (guitar), Tatsuo Hayashi (drums), Masataka Matsutoya (keyboards). Used in 2013 as a theme for the film The Wind Rises; the song dates from 1973. Year is the album release.

original_instruments: Electric guitar | Drums | Bass | Keyboards | Alto saxophone | Trumpet | Trombone | Tenor saxophone | Baritone saxophone
research_notes: Opening track of Tatsuro Yamashita's album For You (AIR/RVC, 21 January 1982). Lyrics Minako Yoshida; music, arrangement and production by Yamashita. Album credits list guitar and percussion (Yamashita), drums (Jun Aoyama), bass (Hiroki Ito), keyboards (Hiroyuki Namba) and a horn section. Not the 1977 album Spacy. Year is the album release.

Written by Miyuki Nakajima; arranged by Ichizō Seo. First released 7 October 1992 on the album East Asia (Pony Canyon). Session credits on the fan discography list drums (Hideo Yamaki), bass (Yasuo Tomikura) and piano/keyboards (Nobuo Kurata). Single-coupled in 1998 with Inochi no betsumei, then used with a TBS drama. Year is the album release.

title_english: Dorawayo Busanhang-e (Come Back to Busan Harbor)
songwriter: 김성술 (lyrics of 돌아와요 충무항에); 황선우 (Busan adaptation)
research_notes: Associated with Cho Yong-pil. The Busan Encyclopedia of Local Culture says the piece adapts Kim Hae-il's 1971 song 돌아와요 충무항에 (lyrics Kim Seong-sul, music Hwang Seon-u), was included on Cho's 1972 album, and became widely known in a 1976 recording with some lyric changes. Cho's official chronology lists 1975. Year left empty because those dates disagree. The encyclopedia calls the style trot-rock.

Title track of Seo Taiji and Boys' debut album, released 23 March 1992 (Bando; Bugs lists the same date). Words, music and production by Seo Taiji. Album track is the Club Mix. Often treated as the start of modern Korean idol dance music; filed here as hip-hop/dance rather than a later K-pop single. Year is the album release.

Sung by Kim Kwang-seok; words and music by Kang Seung-won. On the fourth album 김광석 네 번째. The Daegu Encyclopedia of Local Culture dates that album to 25 June 1994. Dong-a Ilbo independently identifies Kang as the writer. Year is the album release.

One of the five surviving pansori madang: the story of Chunhyang and Yi Mong-ryong, sung by one sorikkun with a buk player. Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and the National Gugak Center both cite Yu Jin-han's 1754 poem in Manhwajip as the oldest surviving literary witness, and say the piece was already sung by the mid-18th century. Shin Jae-hyo later revised pansori texts. No single composer. A full performance is several hours; famous passages include Ssukdaemeori. Decade marks that documented circulation, not a composition year.

title_english: Erquan Yingyue (The Moon Reflected in the Second Spring)
research_notes: Erhu piece by Hua Yanjun (Abing) of Wuxi. The Abing article says it was composed around the late 1930s and had no fixed title until Yang Yinliu and Cao Anhe recorded it on 2 September 1950, when the name Erquan Yingyue was agreed. The piece page confirms the 1950 naming. Exact composition year is not stated, so year is empty and the decade follows the 'late 1930s' estimate. Abing also left the pipa pieces Da lang tao sha, Longchuan and Zhaojun chusai.

title_english: Yi wu suo you (Nothing to My Name)
research_notes: Words and music by Cui Jian. First public performance 9 May 1986 at the International Year of Peace concert in Beijing Workers' Stadium, with the band ADO; that performance was included on the July 1986 compilation 让世界充满爱. Later on the 1989 album 新长征路上的摇滚 (overseas title Nothing to My Name). Mixes rock with northern Chinese folk elements. Year is the first public performance, not the 1989 album.

On Jay Chou's album 我很忙 (JVR Music, 2 November 2007). Music by Chou, lyrics by Vincent Fang, arrangement by Zhong Xingmin. Won Song of the Year at the 19th Golden Melody Awards (2008); the awards archive and Sina both record that prize. Uses a pentatonic gong-mode melody described on the song page as 宫调式. Year is the album release.

title_english: Hoi fut tin hung (Boundless Oceans, Vast Skies)
research_notes: Cantonese rock song by Beyond. Words, music and lead vocal by Wong Ka-kui; arrangement credited to Beyond and Tatsuhiko Hara (梁邦彥). First on the album 樂與怒, stated as 14 May 1993, recorded April 1993 at Fuji Studio, Tokyo. A Japanese version, 遥かなる夢に, was also recorded. Wong died in Tokyo on 30 June 1993. Only one Wikipedia language edition was opened, so verification stays partial. Year is the album release given on that page.

This record documents the long-song form, not one fixed melody. UNESCO (inscribed 2008; proclaimed 2005, joint China and Mongolia) describes a highly ornamented, free-rhythm lyrical chant with falsetto and a wide range, sung at weddings, a new home, a birth, foal-branding and Naadam, distinct from the short song (bogino duu). A specific named long song was not verified in this pass. Also practised in Inner Mongolia, so China is a secondary association. Country of the record is Mongolia.

Debut single of the Ulaanbaatar band The Hu, formed in 2016. Wikipedia places the song in 2018 and on the 2019 album The Gereg; 7digital lists a Dashka Productions release dated 14 October 2018. The band's own YouTube upload is the audio link. The band describes the style as hunnu rock and uses morin khuur, tovshuur and throat singing; a named songwriter was not on the pages consulted. Individual composer credit left empty.

Min'yō of Esashi, Hiyama, Hokkaido, a designated prefectural intangible folk cultural property. Japanese Wikipedia and the town site trace it to Shinano packhorse song carried north by kitamaebune sailors and fused with Kenryō-bushi; the Agency for Cultural Affairs summary says the same. The standard hon-uta begins かもめの鳴く音に. A seven-line score was fixed in 1911; the Esashi Oiwake Association unified schools in 1935. No single composer. Shakuhachi is the usual accompaniment of the formalized song.

Okinawan children's song in ryūka metre. Author and place of origin unknown, according to Japanese Wikipedia and the Okinawa prefectural site. Tinsagu is the balsam flower; the first verse compares a parent's teaching to dye on the nails. Okinawa designated it the prefectural favourite song Uchinaa kanasaata on 18 March 2012. Texts vary by district. English Wikipedia notes sanshin sheet music. Later used in the film Japanese Story; not written for that film.

Classical shakuhachi honkyoku depicting a crane raising a chick until the parent dies. Kotobank says the composition date is unknown and that many temples transmit different melodies under this name. In Kinko-ryū the related piece is called 巣鶴鈴慕. The shakuhachi article notes that Gorō Yamaguchi's performance of Sokaku reibo is on the Voyager Golden Record. Separate kokyū and jiuta pieces share the title and are not this record. A specialist site's claim that Ihara Saikaku mentions the name by 1687 was not confirmed on the encyclopedia pages, so no year is entered.

title_english: Kimi wa tennen-shoku (You Are Natural Color)
research_notes: Opening song of Eiichi Ohtaki's album A Long Vacation and a 7-inch single, both released 21 March 1981 (Niagara/CBS Sony). Lyrics Takashi Matsumoto, music Ohtaki, arrangement credited to Tarō Bannai. The single cuts the album introduction. Later used in the 2020 film Watashi o kuitomete; the song dates from 1981. Artist name is also written 大瀧詠一. Year is the release date.

original_instruments: Keyboards | Clarinet | Alto saxophone | Tenor saxophone
research_notes: 13th single by Spitz, Polydor, released 10 April 1996 (official site and Oricon). Words and music by Masamune Kusano; arrangement Masanori Sasaji and the band. Wikipedia's personnel list for the recording includes keyboards (Sasaji), clarinet (Jake H. Concepcion) and saxophones. No tie-up at release. Year is the single release. Catalogue numbers differ between the official site (POCH-1985) and one Oricon page (PODH-1305); the date agrees.

Written by Shin Jung-hyeon. Korean Wikipedia dates the track to 25 August 1974 on the band album. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says it opened side A of 신중현과 엽전들 1집 (1974), uses electric-guitar and bass riffs, and mixes rock with gugak and folk gestures. Banned 9 July 1975 and lifted 18 August 1987 (English Wikipedia). A film later used the song; it was written as a band track. Year is the 1974 release.

Title song of Yoo Jae-ha's only album, Seoul Records, 20 August 1987. He wrote, composed and arranged the album. English and Korean Wikipedia say this song was first released in 1985 on Cho Yong-pil's seventh album, then sung by Yoo himself because the earlier setting did not match his style. Bugs notes a violin opening. Discogs lists the 1987 LP (SPDR-070) with this as track B4. Year is Yoo's album release, not the 1985 Cho recording.

Title track of IU's EP Real, released 9 December 2010 (Loen). Lyrics Kim Eana, music Lee Min-soo, producer Jo Young-chul. Asia Economy describes violin, brass, guitar and organ solos answering the vocal. Not written as a drama theme. Year is the release date. Artist name IU (Lee Ji-eun).

Martial pipa piece on the Battle of Gaixia (202 BC), told from the Han side. Chinese Wikipedia says a Ming piece called 楚汉 is the early form and that the score titled 十面 was first printed in Hua Qiuping's 1818 pipa collection (10 sections); later scores use the name 十面埋伏 and often 13 sections, of which modern players usually stop at section 10 (Wu River suicide). English Wikipedia agrees on the 1818 printing and the Ming Chu-Han predecessor. No composer. 1818 is a publication date, not entered as a composition year. Paired traditionally with the civil pipa piece 春江花月夜.

Large guqin piece, also called 广陵止息 and associated in qin lore with Nie Zheng's assassination story. Ji Kang (223–263) played a piece of this name before his execution in 263 and said it would be lost. The surviving notation is not securely his: the earliest extant score is in Zhu Quan's Ming handbook 神奇秘谱, which claims a Sui palace source. Tuning is man-shang diao (second string lowered to match the first). Section titles in that score include 取韩, 冲冠 and 投剑. No composition year is entered.

Love song from the Kham region of western Sichuan, built on a local liuliu tune (跑马溜溜的山上) with a Tibetan-derived filler syllable. Chinese Wikipedia says Wu Wenji collected it in 1946 and adapted it under the Kangding title, Jiang Dingxian wrote an accompaniment, and soprano Yu Yixuan sang it publicly in 1947. A competing claim that Li Yiruo of Xuanhan wrote words and music in the 1930s is argued by the Sichuan provincial-chronicles site and rejected, on different evidence, by the Wikipedia article citing the Kangding gazetteer. Authorship is therefore not assigned. No single year is entered. The 1940s decade refers to the circulated concert arrangement, not the folk tune's origin.

title_english: Bāng Chhun-hong (Longing for the Spring Breeze)
research_notes: Hokkien popular song from Japanese-ruled Taiwan. Music Teng Yu-hsien, lyrics Lee Lin-chiu, arrangement Niki Takio, sung by Sun-sun (Liu Qingxiang) for Columbia Records. Chinese Wikipedia says it was recorded in Tokyo in August–September 1933 and issued in early 1934. The National Museum of Taiwan History audio page says recorded September 1933 and issued as a record at the end of 1933 (Columbia 80283). Year 1933 follows the recording; the disc date is given as 1933 or 1934 depending on the source. A 1938 film of the same name came later. Genre name Taiwanese popular song is used because the taxonomy has no Hokkien-pop heading.

Cantonese song by Beyond. Music and Cantonese lyrics by Wong Ka-kui, written in 1990 about Nelson Mandela after his release from prison. Wong's Wikipedia page and the Beyond page both place it on the September 1990 album 命運派對 and record the 1990 Jade Solid Gold best-lyrics prize. A Mandarin version with different lyricists appeared on the April 1991 album of the same name. BBC interviewed Wong Ka-keung on the Mandela dedication. Year is 1990 for the Cantonese release; the exact day 6 September appears on Baidu and is not used.

Track 5 of Eason Chan's Cantonese album U87 (Cinepoly, 7 June 2005). The album Wikipedia table credits lyrics to Wyman Wong (黃偉文), music and arrangement to C.Y. Kong (江志仁), and production to Alvin Leong. Baidu agrees on those credits and the date, and says the working title was Depression. Third plug track of the album. Year is the album release.

This record is the vocal practice, not one fixed melody. UNESCO inscribed Mongolia's khöömei in 2010. A singer holds a drone and a melody of harmonics at once. Two main styles are kharkhiraa (deep, with a subharmonic) and isgeree (whistled overtones). Sung at ceremonies, in the household, while herding, and as a lullaby, learned orally. Origin placed by UNESCO in the Altai of western Mongolia. A separate 2009 inscription covers khoomei as practised in several countries including Inner Mongolia; this record follows the Mongolia nomination.

songwriter: 방시혁 | RM | 슈가 | ADORA | Arlissa Ruppert | Peter Ibsen | Pdogg
research_notes: Lead single from BTS's repackage You Never Walk Alone, released 13 February 2017 (Big Hit). English Wikipedia credits songwriting to Pdogg, RM, Adora, Bang Si-hyuk, Arlissa Ruppert, Peter Ibsen and Suga, produced by Pdogg. The Korean album page lists the same names on track 15. The official music video is directed by YongSeok Choi; the song itself is not a film score, though the video cites literary and film imagery. Year is the single release. Audio URL is the official Big Hit upload returned by search.

Track 10 of Mayday's album 愛情萬歲 (Rock Records, 7 July 2000). The album page says all lyrics and music are by Ashin (Chen Hsin-hung) and arrangements by Mayday. Baidu agrees and says the introduction uses five piano notes. Also used as the ending theme of the TTV serial 俠女闖天關; the song is an album track, not a commissioned score. Named one of the ten singles of 2000 by the Association of Music Workers in Taiwan. Year is the album release.

Guqin piece linked in legend to Bo Ya and Zhong Ziqi, but Chinese Wikipedia says the oldest surviving scores of 高山 and 流水 are in the Ming handbook 神奇秘谱 and are not securely Bo Ya's. By the Tang the old piece had split into two. The version usually played now is the Qing Sichuan qin player Zhang Kongshan's, with the 'seventy-two rolling-and-brushing' passage. Guan Pinghu's recording of the Tianwenge score was placed on the Voyager Golden Record in 1977. This record is 流水, not the separate piece 高山 and not Hou Zuowu's later combination of the two. No composition year.

An upopo (seated song) of the Biratori area, presented by the National Institute for Japanese Language and Linguistics as one of the songs most often sung there. The institute glosses the opening cupka wa kamuy ran as a god descending from the east and alighting on an ash-tree branch. Upopo are sung seated in a circle, often beating a lacquered sintoko lid, sometimes in staggered ukouk. Kotobank and the Ainu-music article describe the form; the named song text is from the institute page only, so the specific lyric attribution is partial. Genre name Ainu music is not in the older taxonomy list.

One of the five surviving pansori madang, distinct from 춘향가. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture and the National Gugak Center describe Sim Cheong sold as a sacrifice so her blind father might see, then returned as empress. A full telling is about four hours. Famous passages include Beompi jungnyu. Late Joseon writings (Gwanuhui and others) mention the piece; a composition year is not given. Shin Jae-hyo later reworked a text. Sung with a buk.

original_instruments: Alto saxophone | Flute | Piano | Electric piano | Electric guitar | Electric bass | Drums | Percussion | Trumpet | Trombone | Tenor saxophone
research_notes: Title track of Sadao Watanabe's album California Shower, released 25 May 1978; recorded March 1978 in Los Angeles (official discography). Personnel there: Watanabe (alto sax, flute, sopranino), Dave Grusin (piano, electric piano), Lee Ritenour (guitar), Chuck Rainey (electric bass), Harvey Mason (drums), Paulinho Da Costa (percussion), Oscar Brashear (trumpet), George Bohanon (trombone), Ernie Watts (tenor sax). A composer credit was not on the official track list or the Victor reissue page, so attribution is Unknown. Japanese Wikipedia notes the track was also heard in the 1978 TV drama 十字路. Year is the album release. Recorded in the United States by a Japanese bandleader.

Min'yō of Tagawa, Fukuoka, from coal-sorting work songs of the Chikuhō pits. Japanese Wikipedia and the Tagawa library trace the familiar melody to the Ita coal-sorting song, arranged in 1910 by the teacher Ono Yoshika as a shamisen piece and first recorded in 1932 by geisha of Gotōji. The city site prints the seichō lyric that includes 月が出た出た 月が出た / 三井炭坑の上に出た. After 1945 the song spread as a bon-dance tune. 1910 and 1932 are arrangement and recording dates, not a composition year, so year is left empty. Several earlier work songs fed the piece.

original_instruments: Piano | Orchestra | Electric guitar | Bass guitar | Drums
research_notes: Ballad by X (later X Japan). English Wikipedia: single 1 December 1989, CBS/Sony, written by Yoshiki, from the album Blue Blood (21 April 1989). The album page says the track uses a full orchestra arranged by Neko Saito and played by Great Eida Strings, and that Yoshiki wrote words and music. Oricon lists the single as the theme of the Toho film Zipang; the song was already on the April album. Artist credited as X, the name on the 1989 release. Piano is part of the band arrangement; a separate published piano score was not confirmed here.

Opening track of Sanulrim's first album, Seorabol Records, 15 December 1977. Words and music by Kim Chang-wan. The band is the three brothers Kim Chang-wan (guitar, vocal), Kim Chang-hoon (bass) and Kim Chang-ik (drums). The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture names this song as the hit from that debut. Hard rock on the album page. Year is the album release.

Hokkien song sung by Sun-sun for Columbia. Music Teng Yu-hsien, lyrics Zhou Tianwang. The melody began as the 1933 children's song 春天 (words Liao Hanchen); Zhou rewrote the lyric as 雨夜花. Chinese Wikipedia and the Teng Yu-hsien digital archive date the release to 1934. The National Museum of Taiwan History says recorded September 1933 and issued about 1934 (Columbia 80300). Year is the release year. Second record for the singer 純純; the composer already appears on 望春風.

Tajik beyit (folk ballad) of the Pamirs. Chinese Wikipedia says the name is both a red flower and a woman's name, and that the song tells of a poor youth who loves a princess of Kabul and wanders singing. Several oral versions exist. The 1963 film song 花儿为什么这样红 is Lei Zhenbang's slowed adaptation of this tune and is not this record. No collector's date is entered as a composition year.

Solo gayageum form with required janggu, in three to six rhythmic movements, lasting about 30 to 60 minutes. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says late-19th-century Kim Changjo (1865–1919) of Yeongam set the framework from sinawi and pansori rhythms, while similar music already existed; eight named schools (ryu) are now transmitted, and the form was designated an Important Intangible Cultural Property in 1968. This record is the tradition, not one school's fixed score. No single year is entered. 1883 is sometimes given as when Kim, then 19, began the form; the encyclopedia treats that as tradition, not a documented premiere.

title_english: Pin pin hei fun nei (I Just Happen to Like You)
research_notes: Title song of Danny Chan's sixth Cantonese album, Warner, August 1983. The song page credits music to Chan, lyrics to Cheng Kwok-kong, arrangement to Joseph Chow, recorded at CBS/Sony Studio in Hong Kong. The album page describes an opening with guzheng and dizi. RTHK Chinese Gold Song of 1983. Not written as a film theme. Year is the album month-year; a day was not given.

This record is the instrument's traditional repertory, not one named tune. UNESCO inscribed Mongolia's morin khuur music in 2008 (proclaimed 2003). A two-string horsehair fiddle with a carved horse head, played solo or with long song, dance, epic and horse ritual. UNESCO notes tatlaga tunes used to tame animals, transmitted orally, and written sources of horse-head fiddles from the Mongol empire of the 13th–14th centuries. A single composition year is not entered.

Shidaiqu written and composed by Li Jinguang, credited on the disc under the pen name Jin Yugu. First sung by Li Xianglan (Yamaguchi Yoshiko) and issued in 1944 by Pathé in Shanghai, according to both the Chinese and Japanese Wikipedia articles. Chinese Wikipedia says Li found the score at a Pathé session after other singers had found the range too wide. A Japanese lyric by Saeki Takao came later. The singer was a Japanese national working in Shanghai; the song is entered under China as a Shanghai popular song. A day of 20 July 1944 appears on Baidu and a video upload, not on the encyclopedia pages, so only the year is used.

Work song of Taketomi Island, Yaeyama, about the beauty Asato Kuyama (1722–1799) and a visiting official. Japanese Wikipedia says yunta were sung without instruments, often as a men's and women's exchange, and that this song is thought to have been joined to a rice-planting song by the early 19th century. English Wikipedia gives the same story. This record is the old song, not the 1934 Columbia version with new standard-Japanese words by Hoshi Katsu and a new melody by Miyara Chōhō, and not the sanshin piece 安里屋節. No composition year is entered.

Words and music by Kim Min-gi. The Encyclopedia of Korean Culture says Yang Hee-eun released it in 1971 on her first album and that Kim included it that autumn on his own first album (Daedo Records). Weekly Hankook describes the Kim recording as piano and strings. Banned in 1975 and lifted in 1987–88. JoongAng dates a first presentation to 28 August 1970; the year entered is the 1971 record. Artist is the singer of the first issued recording.

Guangdong instrumental piece by Lü Wencheng, named as his representative work on his biography page. The piece article says the score appears in Shen Yunsheng's 1938 Qinxian yuepu, in D gong, 2/4. The Hong Kong Windpipe ensemble, working from a Pathé disc, says a 1936 recording (50576b) has Lü on gaohu (then called erhu), Liang Yizhong on yehu, Shao Tiehong on pipa and Lin Haoran on piano, and that a Western-band recording exists from 1935. 1938 is a publication date, so year is left empty. Later used as the first theme of the Hong Kong series Below the Lion Rock; not written for that series. Peng Xiuwen later scored it for a Chinese orchestra.

title_english: Sha si na ge Shijiazhuang ren (Kill That Man from Shijiazhuang)
research_notes: Song by Omnipotent Youth Society. Chinese Wikipedia: lyrics Ji Geng, music and vocal Dong Yaqian, written July 2006, issued on the self-released album 万能青年旅店 on 12 November 2010. The same page describes mandolin in the introduction and trumpet and saxophone at the climax. The YouTube topic upload repeats the 2010-11-12 date and the same credits. Year is the album release, not 2006. Audio URL is the topic upload returned by search, not an independently verified official channel beyond that credit line.

Min'yō of the Tsugaru district, Aomori, one of the Tsugaru mittsu-mono, sung with tsugaru-jamisen and also played as shamisen alone. Japanese Wikipedia says the tune grew from the Hokuriku song Shinbo Kōdaiji kuzushi, and that Kuroishi tells a separate legend tying the name to the 1597 death of the monk Jōen. The Japan Folk Song Association repeats the 1597 story. Old, middle and new performance styles are distinguished. No single composition year is entered, and the 1597 date is a local legend rather than a documented premiere.

Love song sung by Jeon Hye-young of the Pochonbo Electronic Ensemble. Music by Ri Jong-o, using a poem by Cho Ki-chon, who died in the Korean War; Yonhap says the poem dates from just after liberation and that Ri set it in the late 1980s. Release dates disagree: Korean Wikipedia says 1992, English Wikipedia says 1990 with a 1991 vinyl single, and the North Korean arts dictionary dates the work to 1989. Year is therefore empty. A man whistles under a woman's window. Genre name North Korean popular song is not in the older taxonomy list.

Guzheng solo. Chinese Wikipedia gives two accounts: Lou Shuhua (1907–1952) arranged it in the mid-1930s from the old piece Gui qu lai, or Jin Zhuonan (1882–1976) arranged Shandong tunes and taught them to Lou. The circulating Lou score shares its first half with Jin's and has a longer second half of its own. Cao Zheng's transcription of Lou's gongche score spread the piece; a 1941 disc is described on the Guzhengwang summary of a research article. The title quotes Wang Bo's Preface to the Pavilion of the Prince of Teng. Authorship is not assigned to one person, and no year is entered. Later electronic-organ versions used as television cues are separate.

Title track of Jacky Cheung's Mandarin album 吻別, PolyGram, 5 March 1993. The song page and the album tracklist agree: lyrics He Qihong, music and arrangement Yin Wenqi. New song, not a rewrite of an earlier Cantonese hit. Song of the Year at the 1993 Taiwan Golden Melody Awards. The singer is from Hong Kong; the album was a Mandarin release aimed at Taiwan and the mainland. Not a film theme.

Erhu solo by Huang Haihuai. The piece article says he wrote it in 1959 and finished it in 1960, drawing on the Mongolian tune Улаан туг (Red Banner) and its Inner Mongolian form 红旗歌, and that he played it at the 1962 Yangcheng gathering and won a third prize and a new-work prize at the 1963 Shanghai Spring erhu competition. His biography page also dates the piece to 1959. Yangqin accompaniment and plucked-string imitation are described in later accounts of the original. Shen Liqun's shorter 1974 revision, made for Min Huifen, is a different version. Year is 1959.

title_english: Kitaguni no haru (Spring in the North Country)
research_notes: Single by Sen Masao, Tokuma / Minoruphone, 5 April 1977, catalogue KA-1050 in the article body and on his discography (the infobox also prints KA-2035). Lyrics Ide Haku, music Endō Minoru, arrangement Kyō Kensuke. Kotobank agrees on the 1977 release and those credits. A migrant worker remembers a parcel from home. Long-seller prize at the 21st Japan Record Awards. Not a drama theme.

Title song of Chyi Yu's first Mandarin album, Synco, 1979. The album Wikipedia tracklist credits lyrics to Sanmao and music to Li Tai-hsiang, and says the lyric was first called 小毛驢. Apple Music's album note places the record in the Taiwan campus-folk movement and repeats those roles. The month is February on Wikipedia, 9 July on Baidu, and 1 January on Apple Music, so only the year is entered. Briefly banned in Taiwan because the line about a faraway home was read as pointing to the mainland.

Lead song of Faye Wong's first Mandarin album 迷, Cinepoly, 8 April 1994. Lyrics Yao Qian, music Huang Guolun, arrangement Nathan Wang. The album page lists an orchestral version and a strings version. Issued under the name 王靖雯 in Taiwan. Later used as an insert in the 1995 Hong Kong film 烈火戰車; the song was written for the album. Singapore best-lyric prize in 1994 went to this song.

Eighth single by Matsuda Seiko, CBS Sony, 21 January 1982 (catalogue 07SH 1112 on the Wikipedia page; the official site lists 10EH-3200 for a later issue of the same release date). Lyrics Matsumoto Takashi, music Kureta Keiho, a pen name of Matsutoya Yumi. B-side 制服. First number-one on Oricon for her, according to the song page's chart line. Not a drama or film theme.

title_english: Chunjiang huayue ye (Spring River Flower Moon Night)
research_notes: Ensemble piece arranged by Liu Yaozhang of the Great Unity Music Society from Wang Yuting's pipa score 浔阳夜月, itself a reworking of the older pipa piece 夕阳箫鼓. The Huain article, written up from Liu's own account, says the arrangement was finished in October 1925 under the provisional title 秋江月 and renamed 春江花月夜 by Zheng Jinwen in spring 1926, with ten section titles. A Sanya University lecture page also dates the Liu and Zheng ensemble version to about 1925. This is not the Tang poem of the same name, and not the solo pipa piece 十面埋伏. Instrument list is the typical sizhu scoring described in the lecture, not a single documented 1925 session sheet. Year is the 1925 completion of the arrangement.

Title track of Anita Mui's fifth Cantonese album, Capital Artists, 7 January 1986, recorded in 1985. Cantonese lyric by Lin Zhenqiang; music credited to Charlie Dore and Julian Littman, an adaptation of Sheena Easton's Strut. Arrangement Luo Di. Jade Solid Gold award for 1985. Other tracks on the album are television or film themes; this title song is the Easton adaptation. Apple Music repeats the 7 January 1986 album date.

Track 9 of Wu Bai and China Blue's album 愛情的盡頭, Magic Stone, 18 June 1996. The album page says every lyric and tune is by Wu Bai and every arrangement is by Wu Bai and China Blue; length 6:31. Baidu's song entry agrees on the date, the credits and Rock Records as the issuing company. The title alludes to Murakami's novel; the song was not written for a film. A different track on the album, Last Dance, was later used in a drama.
